newsitem.title: USA: New power market threatens 37 nuke plants - study.
newsitem.headline: New power market threatens 37 nuke plants - study.

text.p: Power market competition could force 37 nuclear power plants to shut down prematurely, which could open a big market for natural gas in power generation, according to a study released Tuesday by the Washington International Energy Group.

"If all 37 sites close down, there would be opportunities for up to 1.55 trillion cubic feet of natural gas use per year in electricity generation, which is equivalent to approximately 45 percent of the natural gas used for electricity generation in 1995," said the study, which was done for the Interstate Natural Gas Association of America.
The 37 nuclear facilities make up about 40 percent or 40,000 megawatts of U.S. nuclear generating capacity.
The report comes at a time when natural gas producers have predicted that as power markets open to competition, natural gas might lose market share as a fuel for electric generation.
Most of the nuclear plants that would be vunlerable are in the Northeast and Midwest, where there is good gas potential.

"These sites are vunlerable to shutdown because the market price each is likely to face in their particular region will be less than their annual production costs, even if prices remain level," the study said.
Production costs were not necessarily the determining factor for sites that were vulnerable. Twenty of the 37 sites were considered low-cost producers.

"Some of the top performing...sites are vulnerable because they are located in regions of projected low market price, and some low performing or high cost sites seem to be viable because of regionally high market prices," the study said.

Eight top performing plants could succumb to competition, it Hatch, Wisconsin Public Service's Kewaunee, Northern States Power's Monticello, Niagara Mohawk Power Co's Nine Mile Point 1, PECO Energy's Peach Bottom, Carolina Power and Light Co's Robinson 2, Southern California Edison's San Onofre.
Those eight sites accounted for almost 9,000 megawatts of capacity.
But a Natural Gas Supply Association spokeswoman said the report ignored arguments that threaten natural gas versus nuclear plants.

NGSA's Charlotte LeGates said if industry restructuring was not mandated by a specific date, and if legislation guaranteed a market share for renewable energy, and clean air laws continued to allow coal plants to emit more pollution than natural gas-fired plants, gas would unable to hold its share in the power generation market.
An energy industry source also questioned the assumption that vulnerable high-cost plants would be shut down for good.

"As in any other industry, when high cost plants go into bankruptcy, their assets are sold to pay back investors," the industry source said. If the new company can run it more efficiently, the plant might stay open. ((Sonali Paul, 202- 898-8320)).
